Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette: Mary, a 78-year-old European-American widow, has lived through significant trauma that continues to affect her daily life. The traumatic event she experienced was a devastating natural disaster—a powerful hurricane—that ravaged her coastal hometown several years ago. During the storm, Mary’s home was severely damaged by high winds and flooding. Though she escaped physical injury, witnessing the destruction of familiar surroundings left an indelible mark on her psyche. Mary's triggers are deeply intertwined with specific elements that remind her of the disaster. The opening or slamming of a door often sends shivers down her spine, evoking memories of the storm’s ferocious winds. She also feels acutely distressed when she hears discussions about people losing loved ones—a frequent topic among survivors who have experienced similar losses in their community. Additionally, the smell of alcohol, which was present at emergency shelters where she sought refuge during the storm, triggers intense anxiety. These triggers are potent because they serve as vivid reminders of the terrifying reality she faced during and after the hurricane. Every time Mary hears a door slam or catches a whiff of alcohol, it feels like the world is crumbling around her once again. This reinforces her negative appraisals that the world is a dangerous place, where devastation can strike at any moment without warning. Mary’s belief in the inherent danger of the world exacerbates her feelings of injustice and shattered beliefs about how the world works. She often thinks about how the event could have been prevented if only better measures were in place, leading to prevention rumination. This rumination is both a coping mechanism and a source of distress, as it keeps the traumatic experience at the forefront of her mind. Compulsive cleaning has become another maladaptive strategy for Mary. Organizing and cleaning her home repeatedly gives her a sense of control over an otherwise chaotic world. However, this behavior also reinforces her memory of the event by keeping the disaster vivid in her thoughts. Each time she cleans, she is reminded of the disorder and chaos she experienced during and after the storm. Mary’s memories are both vivid and surreal. At times, she can recall the hurricane with crystal clarity but feels completely numb as if it happened to someone else—a stranger. The memory also feels present rather than something that has passed. This dissonance makes her question reality, further cementing her belief in an unfair world where such extreme events can occur. Mary’s efforts to erase the memory of the event only serve to intensify its presence in her mind. Her compulsive cleaning and rumination about prevention are attempts to regain control but ultimately reinforce her feelings that the world is unsafe and unjust. These maladaptive strategies perpetuate a cycle where Mary feels more trapped by her memories, which in turn trigger her anxiety. The cumulative impact of these symptoms has affected Mary’s daily life, especially as a graphic designer. She avoids social gatherings and discussions about natural disasters at work, which has strained her relationships with colleagues. Her husband tries to be supportive but struggles to understand why she is so distressed by seemingly minor triggers. Mary's journey to seek help came after an incident where the smell of cleaning products triggered intense anxiety during a work event, causing her to leave abruptly and miss an important presentation. This incident made her realize that the trauma was not just affecting her personally but also her professional life. She hopes for a way to reclaim control over her memories and reduce the frequency and intensity of her triggers. Mary is afraid that she will never fully recover from the trauma and that the world will always feel like it’s about to collapse around her. However, she is hopeful that with help, she can find ways to manage her symptoms and regain a sense of safety and control in her life.
